headline: High: Replit Agent can write a shared Repl workspace while TREK handles secrets and collaborative state, creating dangerous default pathways for leakage, conflicts, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Replit Agent can read/write Repl workspace files and TREK exposes collaborative files and MCP/WebSocket surfaces, so a content-to-instruction bridge is plausible if one agent consumes the other's output as trusted text. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than observed.
conditions: IF TREK ingests Replit-written files or MCP payloads as instructions without provenance checks, injection becomes active.
IF the two agents share a writable workspace or synced document, prompt content can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Disable automatic instruction-following on imported files.
Add provenance tags to inter-agent artifacts.
Use separate folders for each agent.
Require human review before one agent consumes the other's output.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Replit Agent touches secrets and deployment configuration in a Repl workspace, while TREK handles API keys, MFA secrets, reservations, and logs in shared files. If either side copies or uploads those artifacts through its networked tools, sensitive data can leave the pair in default workflows.
conditions: IF Replit workspace files contain secrets or deployment config and are read into TREK, leakage risk is active.
IF TREK logs or uploads reservation/API-key data while Replit Agent has network egress, exfiltration becomes plausible.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared files.
Rotate any API keys used in shared workflows.
Restrict network egress for one agent during handoff.
Store sensitive artifacts in separate secret managers.
Review logs for accidental secret capture.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Replit Agent has filesystem write, shell, subprocess, and git mutation in a persistent Repl filesystem; TREK is collaborative and writes to ./data/travel.db, ./uploads/, and logs. Concurrent writes to overlapping mutable state can corrupt files or git history, and no locking mechanism is documented.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same repository or data directory, file races can occur.
IF either agent modifies git state while the other edits the same tree, history conflicts are likely.
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories per agent.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Use git branches for each agent.
Add file locks around shared mutable resources.
Snapshot the workspace before concurrent edits.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Replit Agent can generate code and modify files, while TREK is a real-time collaborative planner with AI built in and can act on shared documents, reservations, or logs. If TREK treats Replit output as authoritative, an upstream mistake can cascade into incorrect travel actions or persisted bad state.
conditions: IF TREK consumes Replit-generated text or code without verification, downstream errors can propagate.
IF either agent writes plans or configs that the other executes, a single mistake can affect multiple work products.
mitigations: Require validation before execution.
Add schema checks to exchanged artifacts.
Keep generated code separate from operational data.
Use a human approval step for actions based on the other agent's output.

E_compliance.rationale: Replit Agent explicitly handles secrets and deployment configuration in a cloud Repl, while TREK handles API keys, MFA secrets, reservations, and user accounts in a self-hosted collaborative app. That combination creates a plausible compliance breach if regulated or account-linked data crosses residency or retention boundaries; the profiles do not show matching controls, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF EU PII, MFA secrets, or reservations are copied from TREK into Replit-managed storage, residency/retention mismatch is active.
IF either agent retains logs or secrets longer than the other, subject-rights handling can diverge.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of cross-agent handoffs.
Document retention for each workspace.
Pseudonymize travel records before transfer.
Review where logs are stored.
Use separate tenants for sensitive data.
